p1.title: Sleep and Memory
p1.text:
Students often stay up late to study before a test. New research suggests this may be a mistake. In one study, two groups of students learned the same list of forty words. One group then slept for eight hours. The other group stayed awake through the night and slept the following day instead.

When both groups were tested, the students who had slept at night remembered about thirty of the words. The students who had stayed awake remembered only nineteen. The researchers believe that during deep sleep the brain strengthens new connections, which helps a person retain what was learned earlier that day.

The finding does not mean that sleep can replace study. Students still have to do the work. But it does suggest that an extra hour of sleep may be worth more than an extra hour of review.

p2.title: The Cost of a Dam
p2.text:
When a large dam is built across a river, the benefits are easy to count. The turbines produce electricity without burning fuel, and the reservoir behind the wall can supply water to cities and farms during a dry season. Governments often present these numbers when they argue for construction.

The costs are harder to measure. A dam blocks the path that migrating fish follow to reach the places where they lay their eggs; in several river systems the fish population has fallen sharply within a decade of construction. Sediment that once travelled downstream and renewed the soil of the floodplain now settles at the bottom of the reservoir instead. Villages below the wall have found that the farmland they depended on grows less each year, a change that was not part of the original plan.

None of this proves that dams should not be built. It does suggest that the question is more complicated than a comparison of electricity produced against money spent.
